text:
**For a full recharge in one day, you need about 270–450 W of solar panels, depending on how much sun you get.** If you can spread it over two days, a 200 W panel is enough.

**The formula:** panel watts ≈ capacity ÷ (peak sun hours × 0.75). The 0.75 allows for losses from heat, panel angle, wiring and the charge controller. Peak sun hours are hours of full-strength sun, not hours of daylight. Most of the US gets about 3–6 a day.

| Peak sun hours | Panel watts for 1,000 Wh in one day |
|---|---|
| 3 hours (winter or cloudy) | about 450 W |
| 4 hours | about 340 W |
| 5 hours | about 270 W |
| 6 hours | about 230 W |

(Source: [Power Station Runtime](https://power-runtime.pages.dev/guides/solar-charging/))

**Slower options:**
- **200 W panel:** It gives about 150 W of real output. That's roughly 6.7 hours of peak sun to fill 1,000 Wh from empty, or about 1.7 days at 4 peak sun hours. ([Enough Watts](https://enoughwatts.com/guides/how-much-solar-to-recharge))
- **100 W panel:** It would take about 3–4 days.

**Check before you buy:**
- **Solar input limit:** Every station caps how much solar it accepts, and extra panel watts beyond that add nothing. Many 1,000 Wh units accept roughly 200–500 W. Look it up on your station's spec sheet.
- **Voltage and current range:** Check this too, especially if you wire panels in series.
- **Plan for your worst month:** Winter sun and shade can cut output a lot.

**A panel to consider:** The [ALLPOWERS SP037 400 W foldable panel](https://dealectric.com/go/allpowers-sp037-400w-solar-panel) is listed at $299. The listing says code ALLPOWERS26 takes $29.90 off, for $269.10. That listing is a deal-site page, so confirm the price at checkout. At 400 W it only helps if your station accepts that much input. If your station's limit is lower, a smaller panel will charge it just as fast.

If you tell me which power station you have, I can check its input limit and suggest a matching panel.

 How much solar to recharge a power station 
 How much solar to recharge a power station
 Panel watts × peak sun hours × 0.75 gives the energy a day. A 200 W panel in 4 hours of peak sun puts back about 600 Wh, as long as the station accepts 200 W of solar input.
 Updated October 6, 2026 
 The formula
 The [solar recharge calculator](/solar-recharge-calculator) and the runtime calculator use the same three steps, stated on the [methodology](/methodology) page:
 Solar input is the smaller of your panel watts and the station's solar input limit.
 Energy a day = solar input × peak sun hours × 0.75.
 Hours of sun to refill = rated capacity ÷ (solar input × 0.75), from empty.
 Worked through on the [Jackery Explorer 2000 v2](/power-stations/jackery-explorer-2000-v2), a 2,042 Wh station with a 400 W solar limit:
 Solar on the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 at 4 peak sun hours Panels Solar input Energy a day Hours of sun to refill Days to refill 
 200 W 200 W 200 × 4 × 0.75 = 600 Wh 13.6 h 3.4 
 400 W 400 W 400 × 4 × 0.75 = 1,200 Wh 6.8 h 1.7 
 600 W 400 W 400 × 4 × 0.75 = 1,200 Wh 6.8 h 1.7 
 The third row shows the cap at work. Panels above 400 W add nothing on this station, so the energy a day stays at 1,200 Wh.
 Peak sun hours squeeze the day of uneven sunlight into the hours of full sun that would deliver the same energy. Peak sun hours, not daylight hours
 Panels deliver their rated watts only in full sun. Morning and evening light gives a fraction of that. Peak sun hours add up the whole day of uneven light and express it as hours of full sun, so a long summer day counts as fewer peak sun hours than it has hours of daylight.
 Our tools start at 4 peak sun hours, a round planning figure, not a claim about your location. Winter, cloud, a low sun angle and shade bring the number down. Enter your own number in either calculator.
 Why 0.75
 A panel rated 200 W rarely puts 200 W into a battery. Hot panels produce less, a panel that is not facing the sun square on catches less light, and the charge controller and wiring lose some on the way. The 0.75 covers those losses in one factor, so 200 W of panels count as 150 W of charging.
 The factor is our assumption, not a measurement. Some days will beat it and some will fall short. We compare your panel watts with the station's limit first and apply the 0.75 after, in the order the methodology states. The refill math also assumes the station charges at the same rate all the way to full.
 The station's solar limit
 Each station accepts a maximum solar input, and the limits in our data run from 100 W on the [BLUETTI Elite 10 Mini](/power-stations/bluetti-elite-10-mini) to 10,000 W on the [EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra X](/power-stations/ecoflow-delta-pro-ultra-x). 42 of the 53 stations with a published limit accept 400 W or more, and 24 accept 1,000 W or more. One station has no published solar limit, and the calculators give no solar figure for it rather than an uncapped one.
 A watt limit is not the only one. Solar inputs also accept a range of voltage and current, which the maker's manual states. We do not check how your panels are wired, so read that range before you connect panels in series.
 Sizing panels to keep up
 To run a setup on solar day after day, the panels must put back what the setup uses. Turn the formula around: panel watts = energy a day ÷ (peak sun hours × 0.75). The table works it out for setups from our scenario pages.
 Panel watts that put back a day of use, rounded up to 10 W Setup Energy a day 3 sun hours 4 sun hours 5 sun hours 
 [A CPAP for two nights](/for/cpap-two-nights) 88 Wh 40 W 30 W 30 W 
 [A refrigerator overnight](/for/refrigerator-overnight) 1,300 Wh 580 W 440 W 350 W 
 [A home office day](/for/home-office-day) 1,436 Wh 640 W 480 W 390 W 
 [Van life](/for/van-life) 1,199 Wh 540 W 400 W 320 W 
 [Outage essentials](/for/outage-essentials) 2,180 Wh 970 W 730 W 590 W 
 Van life is the clearest case: 1,199 Wh a day needs about 400 W of panels at 4 sun hours, and 42 of the 53 stations with a published limit accept that much input. Below that, the battery drains a little each day and the gap grows until a wall or car charge closes it.
 Questions
 How long does a 200 W panel take to recharge a power station? On a station that accepts at least 200 W of solar input, divide the capacity by 150 W, the 200 W panel times 0.75. A 1,000 Wh station takes about 6.7 hours of peak sun from empty, a 2,000 Wh station about 13.3. At 4 peak sun hours a day that is 1.7 and 3.3 days.
 Do more panels than the solar input limit charge faster? No. We cap the input at the station's limit, as the station does. On the [Jackery Explorer 2000 v2](/power-stations/jackery-explorer-2000-v2), with a 400 W limit, 600 W of panels harvest the same 1,200 Wh a day as 400 W. Extra panels can still help on cloudy days, when each panel gives less than its rating, but the calculator does not model that.
 How many solar watts keep up with a refrigerator? A typical modern refrigerator uses 1,300 Wh a day in our data. At 4 peak sun hours, keeping up takes about 440 W of panels: 1,300 ÷ (4 × 0.75), rounded up. At 3 sun hours it takes 580 W.

 How many solar watts to recharge a power station?
 To refill a station in one day, divide its capacity by the peak sun hours you get, then allow for real-world losses. Panels rarely make their rated power; about 75% is a fair planning figure once heat, angle and charging losses are counted.
 Panel watts ≈ capacity ÷ (peak sun hours × 0.75) 
 Panel watts for a full recharge in one day
 Station 3 sun hours 4 sun hours 5 sun hours 6 sun hours 
 500 Wh 230 W 170 W 140 W 120 W 
 1,000 Wh 450 W 340 W 270 W 230 W 
 1,500 Wh 670 W 500 W 400 W 340 W 
 2,000 Wh 890 W 670 W 540 W 450 W 
 Peak sun hours
 A peak sun hour is one hour of full-strength sunlight. Most of the US gets about 3 to 6 a day depending on season and location, with winter and cloudy regions at the low end. Plan with your worst month, not the average.
 Check the station’s solar input
 Every station caps how many solar watts it accepts, commonly somewhere between 200 and 1200 W, and the voltage range of the panels. Panels beyond that limit add nothing. Both figures are on the station’s spec sheet.
